planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Jomanda is a compact, heavily branched ball dahlia that produces an unusually large number of blooms per plant, making it a favorite for cutting.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. Jomanda bears perfectly formed, tightly packed ball-shaped blooms in a bright, warm orange that hold their shape well both on the plant and in the vase, opening from an already generous branching habit that keeps new buds coming in steady succession all season. It is widely grown by cut-flower growers specifically for the sheer volume of usable stems it produces from a single tuber. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new flowers coming, and stake plants in exposed sites since the dense flower heads can weigh down stems in wind. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Franz Kafka is a classic pompon dahlia prized for its perfectly round, honeycomb-textured miniature blooms on a compact, floriferous plant.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Franz Kafka is a true pompon dahlia, its small, densely quilled florets curling inward to form an almost perfectly spherical lavender-purple globe barely 2 inches across, a striking contrast to the huge dinnerplate types grown for size. The dainty, uniform blooms are produced in great abundance on wiry stems, making them a favorite for posies, buttonholes, and mixed bouquets where scale matters. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming through the season, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Park Princess is an unusually vigorous, compact cactus dahlia that can be grown from seed as well as tubers and often blooms its first season.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up, or start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost for first-year bloom. Park Princess produces cheerful cyclamen-pink cactus-type blooms with narrow, quilled petals on compact, well-branched plants that need less staking than taller cactus dahlias. Its shorter stature and seed-grown vigor have made it a long-time favorite for borders and cutting beds alike, blooming freely from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or simply treat as an annual and start fresh from seed each year.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Gallery Art Deco Dahlia (Compact Bronze-Orange Patio Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost, or grow in a large container; Gallery Art Deco is part of the dwarf Gallery series bred specifically for compact borders and patio pots.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep in the garden or a large container; unlike tall border and cutting dahlias, Gallery series dahlias rarely need staking thanks to their naturally dwarf, sturdy habit. Gallery Art Deco carries fully double decorative blooms blending bronze, orange, and gold tones on a compact plant well suited to the front of a border, mixed container, or small bed where taller dahlias would overwhelm the space. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the long summer-to-frost flowering going, and feed lightly, since Gallery types are bred to stay short and heavy fertilizing can encourage floppy, oversized growth. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Mei-Kyo is a hardy pompon-type garden chrysanthemum noted for blooming later and longer into fall than most hardy mums.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to promote bushy growth and heavy budding. Mei-Kyo produces small, tightly packed, rose-pink pompon flowers that gradually deepen to a warm bronze-copper as they age, so a single flush of bloom shows several colors at once late in the season. It is among the latest and longest-blooming of the hardy garden mums, often still flowering well after a light frost when most other perennials have finished for the year. Unlike disposable florist mums, it is a genuinely perennial garden plant that returns and spreads slowly for years; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Bronze Elegance Chrysanthemum (Hardy Warm-Bronze Button Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Bronze Elegance is a hardy button-type garden chrysanthemum long grown as a genuinely perennial fall-blooming mum rather than a disposable florist pot mum.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to encourage bushy, well-budded growth rather than tall, floppy stems. Bronze Elegance bears small, densely packed button flowers in a warm, coppery bronze that pairs naturally with the oranges and golds of the autumn garden, opening over a long stretch from early to mid fall. As a true garden-hardy chrysanthemum it returns reliably for years and slowly bulks up into a substantial clump, unlike short-lived florist mums bred purely for pot sales. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Matchsticks is a spider-type chrysanthemum with distinctive tubular quill petals rather than flat rays.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a bushy, well-budded plant. Matchsticks is instantly recognizable among garden mums for its unusual spidery flower form, with narrow, tubular red petals tipped in bright yellow that curl and hook at the ends, giving the whole bloom a fireworks-like appearance quite unlike the flat, layered petals of typical daisy-form mums. It flowers in mid to late fall and makes an excellent, long-lasting cut flower thanks to its sturdy stems and unusual texture. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Will's Wonderful Chrysanthemum (Hardy Bronze-Red Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Will's Wonderful is a reliably cold-hardy garden mum bred for garden persistence rather than florist pot display.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a compact, heavily budded plant instead of tall, sparse growth. Will's Wonderful bears semi-double, bronze-red daisy flowers with a warm, glowing tone in mid fall, on a plant selected specifically for the ability to survive cold winters in the open garden rather than be discarded after a single season like most florist pot mums. Its dependable hardiness has made it a longtime favorite among gardeners building a true perennial fall border rather than replanting mums every year. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Venus Chrysanthemum (Hardy Korean-Type Single Pink Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Venus is a Korean-type hardy chrysanthemum valued for its simple single daisy form and reliable garden hardiness.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build bushy, well-branched growth loaded with buds. Venus produces clear, soft pink single daisy flowers with a yellow center, a simple and graceful form descended from the tough Korean hybrid mums bred for garden hardiness rather than the double, ball-shaped blooms of florist pot mums. It flowers reliably in fall and, as a genuinely perennial garden plant, spreads gradually into a substantial clump over the years rather than needing yearly replacement. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Ryan's Pink Chrysanthemum (Hardy Soft Pink Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Ryan's Pink is a hardy garden mum grown for genuine perennial garden performance rather than one-season florist pot display.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a compact, heavily budded plant. Ryan's Pink bears soft, clear pink semi-double daisy flowers in mid fall on a sturdy, well-branched plant selected for its ability to survive winters in the ground and return reliably the following year. Its gentle color works well massed in a fall border alongside asters, ornamental grasses, and goldenrod. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and free-flowering.

common_name: Country Girl Chrysanthemum (Hardy Korean Single Rose-Pink Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Country Girl is a vigorous Korean hybrid chrysanthemum bred for cold hardiness and naturalistic single-flower form.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to keep growth bushy rather than tall and floppy. Country Girl produces abundant single, rosy-pink daisy flowers with a golden center in mid to late fall on a vigorous, spreading plant descended from the tough Korean hybrid mums bred specifically for garden hardiness rather than florist pot sales. It naturalizes readily into a substantial, long-lived clump and provides some of the last significant color of the gardening year. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower quality.

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season; Atom is a 1946 heirloom gladiolus still grown today.

directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; stake or plant in blocks to support the flower spikes as they open. Introduced in 1946 and still widely grown, Atom bears small, brilliant red blooms edged with a narrow, glowing silver-white picotee margin, a striking and unusually refined color combination compared to the larger, single-color spikes of most modern gladiolus. Its smaller flower size and wiry stems make it especially good for mixed cut arrangements rather than the bold, oversized spikes typical of exhibition types. Cut spikes once the lowest florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm, and lift and store corms after foliage yellows in colder zones.
sources: American Daffodil and Gladiolus Societies archives

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season; Green Woodpecker is prized among flower arrangers for its rare true-green color.

directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes as the heavy blooms open. Green Woodpecker is one of the few gladiolus cultivars to produce genuinely chartreuse-green blooms, each ruffled floret marked with a deep maroon-red throat blotch that makes the unusual color pop even more. Florists and flower arrangers prize it for adding a true green note to mixed arrangements, a color otherwise scarce among cut flowers. Cut spikes once the lowest florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm, and lift and store corms after foliage yellows in colder zones.

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season; Peter Pears was named for the English tenor and remains a favorite warm-toned exhibition and cutting gladiolus.

directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes as the ruffled blooms open. Peter Pears carries warm apricot-orange florets accented by a deeper red-orange throat blotch, a rich, glowing color that has kept it popular for both garden display and exhibition since its introduction. The tall, densely flowered spikes open from the bottom up over one to two weeks, giving a long window for cutting. Cut spikes once the lowest florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm, and lift and store corms after foliage yellows in colder zones.

common_name: Violet Queen Spider Flower (Deep Violet-Purple Heirloom Cleome)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Violet Queen is the deep purple member of the classic Queen series of spider flower and self-sows readily once established.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Violet Queen is the richest, deepest-colored member of the classic Queen series of spider flower, its large, airy flower heads opening a saturated violet-purple with the same long, protruding stamens that give every cleome bloom its spidery look. Like its Rose Queen and Cherry Queen relatives it shrugs off the worst of Gulf South summer heat, growing vigorously through July and August when many other annuals stall, and blooming continuously from the top of each elongating stem until frost. The slightly sticky, aromatic foliage is typical of the species, and established plantings self-sow freely, drawing hummingbirds, butterflies, and sphinx moths all summer.

common_name: Earl Grey Larkspur (Smoky Lavender-Grey Double Larkspur)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in the Gulf South for spring bloom, or as soon as soil can be worked in colder climates; larkspur seed needs a cool period to germinate well and resents summer heat.

directions: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter gardens, or as early as the ground can be worked in colder climates, since larkspur seed germinates best in cool soil and struggles once summer heat arrives. Earl Grey stands out among larkspur cultivars for its unusual smoky, muted lavender-grey double florets packed densely along tall, airy spires, a subdued, sophisticated color that pairs beautifully with pinks, whites, and dusty blues in a cutting garden. Like other larkspur it finishes its bloom cycle before the worst summer heat and is best treated as a cool-season annual, self-sowing readily where happy. Cut for fresh arrangements when about a third of the spike has opened, or let plants set seed to return the following year; note that all parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Buddy Purple Gomphrena (Dwarf Purple Globe Amaranth)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Buddy Purple is a dwarf, compact gomphrena bred for uniform edging and bedding use.

directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; gomphrena thrives in heat and shrugs off drought once established. Buddy Purple is a compact selection of globe amaranth bearing small, clover-like, rich purple flower heads in dense abundance on tidy, uniform mounds, making it a reliable choice for edging, mass bedding, and containers where taller gomphrena would sprawl. The papery flower heads hold their color for months in the garden and dry beautifully for everlasting arrangements when cut and hung upside down. It blooms non-stop from early summer through frost with no deadheading required and needs little beyond occasional watering during extended dry spells.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers
